{{Short description|Finnish biologist (born 1963)}}
[[File:Jernvall Jukka.jpg|thumb|Jukka Jernvall]]
'''Jukka Jernvall''' (born 1963) is a Finnish [[evolutionary biologist]] in the field of [[evo-devo]] research.<ref>[http://www.aka.fi/en-gb/A/Academy-of-Finland/Who-we-are/Academy-Professors/Academy-Research-Fellows/Jukka-Jernvall-/ Presentation of Jernvall's research in Academy of Finland] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110928203716/http://www.aka.fi/en-gb/A/Academy-of-Finland/Who-we-are/Academy-Professors/Academy-Research-Fellows/Jukka-Jernvall-/ |date=2011-09-28 }}</ref> His research has centered on the interplay of [[ecology]], [[evolution]] and [[developmental biology]], especially of the mammalian [[dentition]]. Jernvall is  currently an [[Academy of Finland#Academy Professors|Academy Professor]]<ref name="lista">{{cite web |url=http://www.aka.fi/fi/akatemia/tutkimuksen-tekijoita/akatemiaprofessorit |title=Akatemiaprofessorit |last1= |first1= |last2= |first2= |date=27 May 2015 |website= |publisher=Academy of Finland |access-date=28 May 2015 |quote= |archive-date=19 April 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190419041554/http://aka.fi/fi/akatemia/tutkimuksen-tekijoita/akatemiaprofessorit/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> at the Institute of Biotechnology, [[University of Helsinki]].<ref>[http://www.biocenter.helsinki.fi/bi/index.html Institute of Biotechnology, University of Helsinki]</ref>

Jernvall received his [[Ph.D.]] in [[evolutionary biology]] in 1995. His thesis investigating the evolution and development of mammalian [[molar (tooth)|molar]] [[Cusp (dentistry)|cusp]] patterns was supervised by [[Irma Thesleff]] and [[Mikael Fortelius]]. This led to the description of [[enamel knot]] as molecular signaling centers in teeth. He also discovered and coined the term ‘secondary [[enamel knot]]’, previously overlooked signaling centers regulating tooth cusp development. This discovery helped to mechanistically link molecular regulation of growth and differentiation to shape. Later, Jernvall has focused on the modelling of three-dimensional dentition [[phenotype]]s. He has studied why certain dentition patterns arise several times during the course of evolution, while other patterns occur only rarely. Jernvall's team has developed several methods from computer modeling of organ development to three-dimensional analysis of biological shape development and function.<ref>[http://www.nature.com/nature/journal/v464/n7288/abs/nature08838.html Salazar-Ciudad I. & Jernvall J. ''Nature'' (2010)]</ref>  Current research ranges from mutant mice in the laboratory to evolutionary diversity in the fossil record and to seal genomics.
